content.heading: 8.1 Affine Combinations
content.paragraph: An affine combination of vectors is a special kind of linear combination. Given vectors (or “points”) $\textbf{v}_{1}$, $\textbf{v}_{2},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ and scalars $c_{1},\ldots,c_{p}$, an affine combination of $\textbf{v}_{1}$, $\textbf{v}_{2},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}$ is a linear combination
such that the weights satisfy $c_{1} + \cdots + c_{p} = 1$.﻿

note.title: ﻿Definition
note.heading: ﻿Definition
note.paragraph: The set of all affine combinations of points in a set $S$ is called the affine hull (or affine span) of $S,$ denoted by $\text{aff~}S$.﻿

content.paragraph: The affine hull of a single point $\textbf{v}_{1}$ is just the set $\left\{ \textbf{v}_{1} \right\}$, since it has the form $c_{1}\textbf{v}_{1}$ where $c_{1} = 1$. The affine hull of two distinct points is often written in a special way. Suppose $\textbf{y} = c_{1}\textbf{v}_{1} + c_{2}\textbf{v}_{2}$ with $c_{1} + c_{2} = 1$. Write $t$ in place of $c_{2}$, so that $c_{1} = 1 - c_{2} = {}$ $1 - t$. Then the affine hull of $\{\textbf{v}_{1},\textbf{v}_{2}\}$ is the set

This set of points includes $\textbf{v}_{1}$ (when $t = 0$) and $\textbf{v}_{2}$ (when $t = 1$). If $\textbf{v}_{2} = \textbf{v}_{1}$, then (1) again describes just one point. Otherwise, (1) describes the line through $\textbf{v}_{1}$ and $\textbf{v}_{2}$. To see this, rewrite (1) in the form

where $\textbf{p}$ is $\textbf{v}_{1}$ and $\textbf{u}$ is $\textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1}$. The set of all multiples of $\textbf{u}$ is $\text{Span}\{\textbf{u}\}\text{,}$ the line through $\textbf{u}$ and the origin. Adding $\textbf{p}$ to each point on this line translates $\text{Span}\{\textbf{u}\}$ into the line through $\textbf{p}$ parallel to the line through $\textbf{u}$ and the origin. See Figure 1. (Compare this figure with Figure 5 in Section 1.5.)

content.paragraph: Notice that while the point $\textbf{y}$ in Figure 2 is an affine combination of $\textbf{v}_{1}$ and $\textbf{v}_{2}$, the point $\textbf{y} - \textbf{v}_{1}$ equals $t\left( \textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1} \right)$, which is a linear combination (in fact, a multiple) of $\textbf{v}_{2} - \textbf{v}_{1}$. This relation between $\textbf{y}$ and $\textbf{y} - \textbf{v}_{1}$ holds for any affine combination of points, as the following theorem shows.

content.paragraph: While the procedure in Example 1 works for arbitrary points $\textbf{v}_{1}$, $\textbf{v}_{2},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$, the question can be answered more directly if the chosen points $\textbf{v}_{i}$ are a basis for ${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$. For example, let $B = \{\textbf{b}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{b}_{n}\}$ be such a basis. Then any $\textbf{y}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ is a unique linear combination of $\textbf{b}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{b}_{n}$. This combination is an affine combination of the $\textbf{b}$’s if and only if the weights sum to $1$. (These weights are just the $B\text{-coordinates}$ of $\textbf{y}$, as in Section 4.4.)

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: A set $S$ is affine if $\textbf{p}$, $\textbf{q} \in S$ implies that $(1 - t)\textbf{p} + t\textbf{q} \in S$ for each real number $t$.﻿

content.paragraph: Geometrically, a set is affine if whenever two points are in the set, the entire line through these points is in the set. (If $S$ contains only one point, $\textbf{p}$, then the line through $\textbf{p}$ and $\textbf{p}$ is just a point, a “degenerate” line.) Algebraically, for a set $S$ to be affine, the definition requires that every affine combination of two points of $S$ belong to $S$. Remarkably, this is equivalent to requiring that $S$ contain every affine combination of an arbitrary number of points of $S$.﻿

note.title: Theorem 2
note.heading: Theorem 2
note.paragraph: A set $S$ is affine if and only if every affine combination of points of $S$ lies in $S$. That is, $S$ is affine if and only if $S = \text{aff~}S$.﻿

content.paragraph: Remark:See the remark prior to Theorem 5 in Chapter 3 regarding mathematical induction.
content.heading: Proof
content.paragraph: Suppose that $S$ is affine and use induction on the number $m$ of points of $S$ occurring in an affine combination. When $m$ is $1$ or $2$, an affine combination of $m$ points of $S$ lies in $S$, by the definition of an affine set. Now, assume that every affine combination of $k$ or fewer points of $S$ yields a point in $S$, and consider a combination of $k + 1$ points. Take $\textbf{v}_{i}$ in $S$ for $i = 1,\ldots,k + 1$, and let $\textbf{y} = c_{1}\textbf{v}_{1} + \cdots + c_{k}\textbf{v}_{k} + c_{k + 1}\textbf{v}_{k + 1}$, where $c_{1} + \cdots + c_{k + 1} = 1$. Since the $c_{i}$’s sum to $1$, at least one of them must not be equal to $1$. By reindexing the $\textbf{v}_{i}$ and $c_{i}$, if necessary, we may assume that $c_{k + 1} \neq 1$. Let $t = c_{1} + \cdots + c_{k}$. Then $t = 1 - c_{k + 1} \neq 0$, and

By the induction hypothesis, the point $\textbf{z} = (c_{1}/t)\textbf{v}_{1} + \cdots + (c_{k}/t)\textbf{v}_{k}$ is in $S$, since the coefficients sum to $1$. Thus (6) displays $\textbf{y}$ as an affine combination of two points in $S$, and so $\textbf{y} \in S$. By the principle of induction, every affine combination of such points lies in $S$. That is, $\text{aff~}S \subseteq S$. But the reverse inclusion, $S \subseteq \text{aff~}S$, always applies. Thus, when $S = \text{aff~}S$. Conversely, if $S = \text{aff~}S$, then affine combinations of two (or more) points of $S$ lie in $S$, so $S$ is affine.
The next definition provides terminology for affine sets that emphasizes their close connection with subspaces of $\text{ℝ}^{n}$.﻿

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: A translate of a set $S$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ by a vector $\textbf{p}$ is the set $S + \textbf{p} = \left\{ \textbf{s} + \textbf{p}:\textbf{s} \in S \right\}$.﻿2 A flat in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ is a translate of a subspace of $\text{ℝ}^{n}$. Two flats are parallel if one is a translate of the other. The dimension of a flat is the dimension of the corresponding parallel subspace. The dimension of a set $S$, written as dim $S$, is the dimension of the smallest flat containing $S$. A line in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ is a flat of dimension $1$. A hyperplane in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ is a flat of dimension $n - 1$.﻿

content.paragraph: In $\text{ℝ}^{3}$, the proper subspaces3 consist of the origin $0$, the set of all lines through $0$, and the set of all planes through $0$. Thus the proper flats in $\text{ℝ}^{3}$ are points (zero-dimensional), lines (one-dimensional), and planes (two-dimensional), which may or may not pass through the origin.

The next theorem shows that these geometric descriptions of lines and planes in $\text{ℝ}^{3}$ (as translates of subspaces) actually coincide with their earlier algebraic descriptions as sets of all affine combinations of two or three points, respectively.

note.title: Theorem 3
note.heading: Theorem 3
note.paragraph: A nonempty set $S$ is affine if and only if it is a flat.

content.paragraph: Remark: Notice the key role that definitions play in this proof. For example, the first part assumes that $S$ is affine and seeks to show that $S$ is a flat. By definition, a flat is a translate of a subspace. By choosing $\textbf{p}$ in $S$ and defining $W = S + \left( - \textbf{p} \right)$, the set $S$ is translated to the origin and $S = W + \textbf{p}$. It remains to show that $W$ is a subspace, for then $S$ will be a translate of a subspace and hence a flat.

content.paragraph: Suppose that $S$ is affine. Let $\textbf{p}$ be any fixed point in $S$ and let

To show that $S$ is a flat, it suffices to show that $W$ is a subspace of $\text{ℝ}^{n}$. Since $\textbf{p}$ is in $S$, the zero vector is in $W$. To show that $W$ is closed under sums and scalar multiples, it suffices to show that if $\textbf{u}_{1}$ and $\textbf{u}_{2}$ are elements of $W$, then $\textbf{u}_{1} + t\textbf{u}_{2}$ is in $W$ for every real $t$. That is, we want to show that $\textbf{u}_{1} + t\textbf{u}_{2}$ is in $S + \left( - \textbf{p} \right)$. Since $\textbf{u}_{1}$ and $\textbf{u}_{2}$ are in $W$, there exist $\textbf{s}_{1}$ and $\textbf{s}_{2}$ in $S$ such that
It follows that

Regrouping the first three terms, we find that $\textbf{s}_{1} + t\textbf{s}_{2} - t\textbf{p}$ is in $S$ since the coefficients sum to $1$ and $S$ is affine. (SeeTheorem 2.) So $\textbf{u}_{1} + t\textbf{u}_{2}$ is in $S - \textbf{p} = W$. This shows that $W$ is a subspace of $\text{ℝ}^{n}$. Thus $S$ is a flat, because $S = W + \textbf{p}$.﻿

Conversely, suppose that $S$ is a flat. That is, $S = W + \textbf{p}$ for some $\textbf{p}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ and some subspace $W$. To show that $S$ is affine, it suffices to show that for any pair $\textbf{s}_{1}$ and $\textbf{s}_{2}$ of points in $S$, the line through $\textbf{s}_{1}$ and $\textbf{s}_{2}$ lies in $S$. So, for each real $t$ we have
Since $W$ is a subspace, $(1 - t)\textbf{u}_{1} + t\textbf{u}_{2}$ is in $W$ and so $(1 - t)\textbf{s}_{1} + t\textbf{s}_{2}$ is in $W + \textbf{p} = S$. Thus, $S$ is affine.

Theorem 3 provides a geometric way to view the affine hull of a set: it is the flat that consists of all the affine combinations of points in the set. For instance, Figure 3 shows the points studied in Example 2. Although the set of all linear combinations of $\textbf{b}_{1}$, $\textbf{b}_{2}$, and $\textbf{b}_{3}$ is all of $\text{ℝ}^{3}$, the set of all affine combinations is only the plane through $\textbf{b}_{1}$, $\textbf{b}_{2}$, and $\textbf{b}_{3}$. Note that $\textbf{p}_{2}$ (from Example 2) is in the plane through $\textbf{b}_{1}$, $\textbf{b}_{2}$, and $\textbf{b}_{3}$, while $\textbf{p}_{1}$ is not in that plane. Also, see Exercise 22.

content.paragraph: Earlier, Theorem 1 displayed an important connection between affine combinations and linear combinations. The next theorem provides another view of affine combinations, which for $\text{ℝ}^{2}$ and $\text{ℝ}^{3}$ is closely connected to applications in computer graphics, discussed in the next section (and in Section 2.7).

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: For $\textbf{v}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$, the standard homogeneous form of $\textbf{v}$ is the point $\overset{}{\widetilde{\mathbf{v}}} = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{v} \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n + 1}$.﻿

note.title: Theorem 4
note.heading: Theorem 4
note.paragraph: A point $\textbf{y}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ is an affine combination of $\textbf{v}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{v}_{p}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ if and only if the homogeneous form of $\textbf{y}$ is in $\text{Span\{}{\overset{\sim}{\textbf{v}}}_{1},\ldots,{\overset{\sim}{\textbf{v}}}_{p}\text{\}}$. In fact, $\textbf{y} = c_{1}\textbf{v}_{1} + \cdots + c_{p}\textbf{v}_{p}$, with $c_{1} + \cdots + c_{p} = 1$, if and only if $\overset{\sim}{\textbf{y}} = c_{1}{\overset{\sim}{\textbf{v}}}_{1} + \cdots + c_{p}{\overset{\sim}{\textbf{v}}}_{p}$.﻿
